findings.quote: Heating a sample therefore makes its particles move faster.
findings.problem: False as a general statement. During a phase change, heat goes in but the particles do not speed up and the temperature stays constant. The lesson itself says so later ("the added energy is used to pull particles away from each other, not to speed them up"), and Trap #6 warns against the very idea this sentence states. A student who heats a pure solid at its melting point and applies this sentence answers that particle motion increases, which is wrong.
findings.source: Checklist B01; reader-rules Sol addition (test every 'so'/'therefore' against a known exception); OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 10.3 Phase Transitions (heating curve: temperature, and so average kinetic energy, constant during melting and boiling)

findings.quote: If the particles move apart (solid to liquid to gas), energy goes in. If they come closer, energy comes out.
findings.problem: The stated rule fails for water, the substance most exam items use. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so its molecules are farther apart on average: melting brings them closer yet takes in energy, and freezing moves them apart yet gives out energy. Students know that water expands when it freezes; applying this rule by spacing gives the wrong energy direction. The only limit given ("This holds when the substance is not reacting") does not cover it. The energy direction follows breaking or forming attractions, not particle spacing; the same spacing framing appears in Core Concept and in Example #6 step 3 about melting ice.
findings.source: Checklist B01; writer-rules 'Word every shortcut and trap with its limit'; OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 10.1 (hydrogen bonding makes ice less dense than liquid water) and 10.3 (fusion endothermic, freezing exothermic)

findings.quote: **homogeneous mixture** looks the same throughout. Salt dissolved in water and air are examples. A homogeneous mixture is often called a **solution**.
findings.problem: The test is given by appearance with no limit, then tied to the word solution. Colloids such as milk and fog look the same throughout but are not solutions, so a student using this definition calls milk a homogeneous mixture or a solution, a common exam choice. The lesson never states this limit, and it conflicts with the sibling lesson lesson-chemistry-mixtures-and-separation, whose Trap #1 warns "A mixture that looks uniform can still be a colloid".
findings.source: Checklist L27; OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 11.5 Colloids (milk listed as a colloid, an emulsion, distinct from a solution); content/lessons/science/chemistry/mixtures-and-separation.md Traps #1

findings.quote: > Plasma has many charged particles. Heat is one way to make them, but it is not the definition.
findings.problem: Trap #3 has only the one-line warning and no short explanation paragraph. Trap #4 ("Mixing Up Evaporation and Boiling") has the same gap. The format needs a warning and a short explanation.

findings.quote: During a phase change, the added energy is used to pull particles away from each other, not to speed them up.
findings.problem: This paragraph has five sentences. Others also exceed three: the paragraph starting "The spacing also explains other behavior." (five), "A compound can be broken down" (four), "A fourth state is **plasma**." (four), and "Signs of a chemical change include" (four). Paragraphs should be one to three short sentences.
